scope_note: Full-source boundary-date probe covering 13 targets and 11 contexts. Bodies, XML date bounds, exclusions, apparatus and source roles were read; all records remain evidence-only and no links are accepted.

record_reviews.summary: Lyell answers a preceding Darwin discussion of heterogeneous subjects and geographic natural history. He recalls Tasmanian zoophytes and Hobart insects resembling temperate or English forms, invokes Beck on Antarctic/Arctic conchology, reports Miocene Virginia fossils, and promises to put Darwin’s Arctic-flora query to Bunbury while describing Bunbury’s carboniferous-plant climate argument. The surviving block ends mid-sentence, so the closing extent is incomplete.
record_reviews.date_assessment: after 2 August 1845; XML bounds 1845-08-03 to 1882-12-31. This boundary record is not period-selection eligible.
record_reviews.attribution_assessment: incoming Lyell voice; reports Gray, Beck, Brown and Bunbury as distinct authorities; body is incomplete at the preserved ending.
record_reviews.unmatched_reason: Darwin’s prior letter is not in this packet; the source is an answer to an unlocated prompt and falls far before the nominal period.

evidence.quote: how like they looked to those on our shore
I will put your query as to that of the arctic region to Charles Bunbury

record_reviews.summary: Lyell discusses post-glacial plant migration, proposed land connections around the Bay of Biscay and Ireland, Jamieson’s five periods, and possible maps for his geological work. He asks whether Hooker criticized Forbes’s botanical migrations and comments on Phillips’s treatment of the Amiens man and transmutation. The opening is a continuation from a missing preceding page, so the surviving text is not a complete letter.
record_reviews.date_assessment: before 20 November 1860; XML bounds 1809-01-01 to 1860-11-19. This boundary record is not period-selection eligible.
record_reviews.attribution_assessment: Lyell-authored incoming; Hooker, Forbes, Phillips, Sedgwick and others are discussed as third parties.
record_reviews.unmatched_reason: The Darwin prompt is missing; the source supplies questions to Darwin rather than a traceable response endpoint in this packet.

evidence.quote: a low plain of land skirting the bay of Biscay & France & joining Ireland
Has Hooker or any one ever criticized E. Forbes’ Botanical migrations

record_reviews.summary: Dorothy Frances Nevill asks Darwin for a photograph or lithograph to hang in her sitting room, citing Hooker and other friends, then says she is interested in his pigeon account and asks whether he lives near Sydney. The damaged first block contains the request and social rationale; the closing and two short additions are preserved.
record_reviews.date_assessment: before 22 January 1862; XML bounds 1809-01-01 to 1862-01-21. This boundary record is not period-selection eligible.
record_reviews.attribution_assessment: Nevill is the author and admirer; Hooker is only a comparison in her request.
record_reviews.unmatched_reason: No Darwin reply or photograph dispatch is preserved; this is an incoming social request, not a scientific prompt matched here.

evidence.quote: give me a photo or lithograph or any other portrait of yourself
I am so interested in the account of your pigeons in your book

record_reviews.summary: D. F. Nevill thanks Darwin for promising a photograph, says it has not yet arrived, and reports a gardener’s observation that a dry Cynoches flower jerks its anther back and ejects pollen onto the pistil. She also says a Pleroma has finished flowering and she will attend to Darwin’s pamphlet.
record_reviews.date_assessment: before 22 January 1862; XML bounds 1809-01-01 to 1862-01-21. This boundary record is not period-selection eligible.
record_reviews.attribution_assessment: Nevill’s report includes an explicitly attributed gardener observation and her own receipt/non-receipt of the photograph; no Darwin prose is present.
record_reviews.unmatched_reason: The promised photograph and Darwin’s preceding letter are not preserved; the botanical observation is not evidence of a dated Darwin reply.

evidence.quote: It has not arrived yet but I must be patient
the anther appears to go quite back with a jerk

record_reviews.summary: Oxenden reports a day searching for Arachnites: only five plants, three flowering, because the season is two or three weeks or a month early; two flowers are enclosed and a third given to Lady Dundonald. He compares this with finding fifty plants two years earlier and notes grazing damage.
record_reviews.date_assessment: before 30 May 1862; XML bounds 1809-01-01 to 1862-05-29. This boundary record is not period-selection eligible.
record_reviews.attribution_assessment: Oxenden is the observer and sender; Lady Dundonald is a recipient of one flower, not a Darwin correspondent.
record_reviews.unmatched_reason: The prior Darwin request or desired specimen purpose is not preserved, so no direct reply is identified.

evidence.quote: It is too Early for them, by two or three weeks—or a Month
I have enclosed two to you, by Post, this day

record_reviews.summary: Oxenden says Darwin is leaving orchid work and that this removes much of the pleasure of chalk-country collecting. He offers newly found Orchis Arachnites in prime condition and Epipactis palustris not flowering for three weeks, asking whether Darwin still wants either.
record_reviews.date_assessment: before 21 June 1862; XML bounds 1809-01-01 to 1862-06-20. This boundary record is not period-selection eligible.
record_reviews.attribution_assessment: Oxenden’s first-person collecting and offer are the surviving voice; the addressee is Darwin.
record_reviews.unmatched_reason: No Darwin answer or receipt of either specimen is preserved; catalogue order and shared orchid subject do not identify a pair.

evidence.quote: quite a new & rich mine of O. Arachnites
So tell me, if you still care to have either

record_reviews.summary: A one-block Ray Society minute records that a Darwin letter suggested translating Gaertner’s Bastardezeugung. It is an institutional record of a proposal, not Darwin’s letter or a transcription of its contents.
record_reviews.date_assessment: before 4 November 1864; XML bounds 1809-01-01 to 1864-11-03. This boundary record is not period-selection eligible.
record_reviews.attribution_assessment: Ray Society minute voice; Darwin’s letter is reported in third person and is not available as body text.
record_reviews.unmatched_reason: The underlying Darwin letter and any incoming prompt are absent; this minute cannot establish composition, receipt or scientific response.

evidence.quote: Read a letter from Mr Darwin suggesting the Translation of Gaertner’s work on “Bastardezeugung”

record_reviews.summary: This Ray Society minute resumes consideration of translating Gaertner, reports that Darwin said the work was not antiquated and that no one could add notes of much value, and records Hooker and Darwin recommending production of an English translation. It ends with the institutional resolution to accept it for an early year.
record_reviews.date_assessment: before 7 January 1865; XML bounds 1809-01-01 to 1865-01-06. This boundary record is not period-selection eligible.
record_reviews.attribution_assessment: Official minute voice; Darwin and Hooker are reported speakers, not authors of the surviving block. The F suffix does not make this a fragment: it is a complete one-block minute transcription.
record_reviews.unmatched_reason: The referenced Darwin letter is not reproduced and no letter-level prompt/response can be inferred from the resolution.

evidence.quote: the work was in no degree antiquated
The production of an English Translation of this work being strongly recommended both by Mr Darwin & Dr Hooker

record_reviews.summary: Buckland’s letter combines an invitation to see salmon hatching and The Field’s request for natural-history queries with a skeptical list of repeated animal stories: viper swallowing young, dog–fox cross and toad-in-a-hole. The body then closes with a playful Latin-style “cum multis aliis” list. The source has a continuation-like opening and the editorially preserved sequence is not a clean single topical answer.
record_reviews.date_assessment: before 1 February 1863; XML bounds 1809-01-01 to 1863-01-31. This boundary record is not period-selection eligible.
record_reviews.attribution_assessment: Buckland’s voice includes The Field editor’s reported request and his own sceptical assessment; no Darwin text is present.
record_reviews.unmatched_reason: The Darwin query is not preserved and the listed anecdotes do not identify a particular Darwin response.

evidence.quote: By the way the Editor of The Field requests me to inform you
people coin a story & tell it so many times that at last they believe it themselves

record_reviews.summary: Frank Buckland discusses river-dependent salmon and trout size, casts of fish, and hatchery plans at Hampton and Galway. He says he quoted Darwin’s book in a £100,000 salmon-arbitration dispute, where the opposing side extrapolated seven years of fishery increase for twenty-eight years; Buckland invokes Darwin’s “elements of self destruction.” He calls the letter a rigmarole and does not supply the underlying legal material.
record_reviews.date_assessment: before 11 December 1864; XML bounds 1809-01-01 to 1864-12-10. This boundary record is not period-selection eligible.
record_reviews.attribution_assessment: Buckland is the author; the arbitration and its opposing side are reported third-party contexts.
record_reviews.unmatched_reason: No Darwin prompt or response is preserved; quotation of Darwin’s book is public-use evidence, not proof of a new incoming letter.

evidence.quote: The other side wanted to make out that if the fishery had increased for seven years, it would go on increasing in same ratio for 28 years

record_reviews.summary: Darwin tells Cresy that Hooker has finally replied after two or three Darwin letters and declines Cresy’s offer of a plant on Hooker’s behalf. This is a short administrative relay, not a scientific answer: Darwin merely reports Hooker’s thanks and lack of need. The catalogue offers disjoint date alternatives (1843–46 or 1855–60), while the displayed day is 26 December 1843.
record_reviews.date_assessment: 26 December 1843; alternative editorial range 26 Dec 1843–Apr 1846 or Sept 1855–Oct 1860; XML bounds 1843-12-26 to 1860-10-26. This boundary record is not period-selection eligible.
record_reviews.attribution_assessment: Darwin-authored outgoing; Hooker’s words are relayed in third person and Cresy’s offer is summarized, not quoted.
record_reviews.unmatched_reason: The relevant Cresy letters are unlocated here; the disjoint date alternatives prevent period placement and no new pair is asserted.

evidence.quote: In answer to 2 or 3 letters of mine I heard only this morning from Dr. Hooker
they do not want any

record_reviews.summary: Crocker thanks Darwin for a long letter and plans experiments on Hollyhocks, Larkspurs and Beaton’s Pelargonium work. He offers wild carrot, celery and beet for comparison, reflects on a possible Linum cutting-versus-seed confound, asks what dimorphous plants to seek in marshy or brackish ground, and declines to state uncertain orchid pollen claims. He closes with a practical-observer philosophy and health news.
record_reviews.date_assessment: before 13 March 1862; XML bounds 1809-01-01 to 1862-03-12. This boundary record is not period-selection eligible.
record_reviews.attribution_assessment: Crocker’s own experimental plans and uncertainty statements are distinct from Darwin’s presumed preceding suggestions; bracketed lacunae remain editorial restorations.
record_reviews.unmatched_reason: Darwin’s long letter is not preserved, so this answer cannot be tied to a particular prompt or receipt stage.

evidence.quote: I shall have much real enjoyment in trying the experiment upon Hollyhocks
it is better to keep silence than to state anything upon which there is a doubt in one’s mind

record_reviews.summary: Daly’s 23-block errata list corrects words, grammar, French and a scientific term across pages of a book, including “bearing,” “more slowly,” “graduate,” “n’en est pas,” “rudimentary,” “insessorial,” and revisions to sentences about varieties, blood, leaf retention and difference. It is a proof-correction memorandum, not a scientific correspondence exchange.
record_reviews.date_assessment: before 9 February 1868; XML bounds 1809-01-01 to 1868-02-08. This boundary record is not period-selection eligible.
record_reviews.attribution_assessment: Daly’s editorial/proofreading voice; the book text and proposed corrections are the object, with no Darwin body prose.
record_reviews.unmatched_reason: The book or covering Darwin request is not represented as a letter endpoint; no direct link is proposed.

evidence.quote: For berning Read bearing
incessorial should, I think, be insessorial

record_reviews.summary: Darwin thanks Cresy for assistance, promises to speak to Owen, De la Beche and Hutton, explains that poor health and Emma’s expected confinement prevented a proposed gathering of naturalists, wishes Cresy success, and notes a Saturday departure for the seaside. It is social/professional support, not a scientific response.
record_reviews.date_assessment: 20 July 1848; XML bounds 1848-07-20 to 1848-07-20. This boundary record is not period-selection eligible.
record_reviews.attribution_assessment: Darwin-authored outgoing; named scientists are prospective intermediaries, not correspondents in the surviving body.
record_reviews.unmatched_reason: Cresy’s preceding scheme is referred to but not preserved in this packet; no period relationship is inferred.

evidence.quote: my wife soon expecting her confinement
I leave home on Saturday for a week to the sea-side

record_reviews.summary: Darwin replies to Cresy’s forwarded letter about Dr King. He refuses to canvass for someone he does not personally know on second-hand information, returns the documents, offers only to mention King to Owen if they meet, and closes with health and travel details.
record_reviews.date_assessment: 24 June 1849; XML bounds 1849-06-24 to 1849-06-24. This boundary record is not period-selection eligible.
record_reviews.attribution_assessment: Darwin-authored outgoing; Cresy’s forwarded documents and Dr King’s testimonials are third-party material, not Darwin’s evidence.
record_reviews.unmatched_reason: The forwarded letter is not a preserved incoming endpoint here; the response is an administrative decision rather than a scientific prompt match.

evidence.quote: it is really impossible that I can canvass for a man not personally known to me
I return the documents to save the trouble of copies

record_reviews.summary: A Ray Society minute records a secretary’s instruction to ask Darwin whether he would agree to publish his cirripede work in parts, beginning with pedunculated cirripeds and related illustrations and anatomy. This is an institutional request record, not the requested letter itself.
record_reviews.date_assessment: after 7 October 1850; XML bounds 1850-10-08 to 1850-10-31. This boundary record is not period-selection eligible.
record_reviews.attribution_assessment: Ray Society institutional voice; Darwin is the requested recipient and subject of the minute, not its author.
record_reviews.unmatched_reason: The actual request letter and Darwin’s response are absent; no direct edge is asserted.

evidence.quote: ask Mr. Darwin if he would agree to the publication of his work in parts

record_reviews.summary: A Ray Society minute states that a letter from Darwin was read and the secretary was instructed to request a specimen plate for Sowerby to estimate cirripede plate costs. It documents a meeting response to Darwin’s letter, not the letter’s text and not delivery of the secretary’s request.
record_reviews.date_assessment: 4–6 November 1850; XML bounds 1850-11-04 to 1850-11-06. This boundary record is not period-selection eligible.
record_reviews.attribution_assessment: Institutional minute voice; Darwin’s letter is summarized in third person and Sowerby is the intended recipient of a plate.
record_reviews.unmatched_reason: The Darwin letter and secretary’s outgoing request are not preserved; this is evidence of institutional action only.

evidence.quote: A letter was read from Mr. Darwin
request him to send a specimen plate to Mr Sowerby

record_reviews.summary: Darwin thanks Cresy for advice on a siphon and tank, adopts a one-end union and plug plan, discusses nine-inch brick ribs and a hose, and says he will ask the Gardeners’ Chronicle only because Cresy’s answer made that unnecessary. He also invites Cresy to visit.
record_reviews.date_assessment: 29 April 1853; XML bounds 1853-04-29 to 1853-04-29. This boundary record is not period-selection eligible.
record_reviews.attribution_assessment: Darwin-authored outgoing; Cresy’s technical section is only reported through Darwin’s response, with no incoming body preserved.
record_reviews.unmatched_reason: The prompt and drawing/section are missing. This is a response to practical advice, but no endpoint is available for a source-complete pair.

evidence.quote: I will try the siphon plan
it now turns out through your kindness quite superfluously

record_reviews.summary: Darwin abandons the siphon plan after visiting Burgess & Key: the coated hose is flat, gutta-percha unsuitable for frequent movement, and leather would cost nearly £20. He will build an ordinary tank with a pump and apologizes for the trouble. This is a change of plan following the earlier technical exchange, not evidence that 1677’s exact incoming section survives.
record_reviews.date_assessment: 15 May 1853; XML bounds 1853-05-15 to 1853-05-15. This boundary record is not period-selection eligible.
record_reviews.attribution_assessment: Darwin-authored outgoing; suppliers’ advice is reported, not a preserved correspondent voice.
record_reviews.unmatched_reason: The earlier Cresy prompt and any receipt of this change are absent; shared tank topic does not establish a new direct edge.

evidence.quote: in despair I have given up the siphon-plan
this would have cost me nearly £20

record_reviews.summary: A Ray Society minute records Darwin stating that the manuscript of volume two of his work extended to 900 pages; the society therefore resolved to publish the whole in one volume. This is a single institutional decision block, not Darwin’s manuscript or a letter transcription.
record_reviews.date_assessment: before 23 January 1854; XML bounds 1809-01-01 to 1854-01-22. This boundary record is not period-selection eligible.
record_reviews.attribution_assessment: Ray Society minute voice reports Darwin’s statement in third person.
record_reviews.unmatched_reason: No underlying Darwin letter or incoming institutional prompt is preserved.

evidence.quote: the Mss of the 2nd. vol of his work extended to 900 pages

record_reviews.summary: Darwin writes to Lyell to answer Lady Lyell’s note to Emma, discusses illness and family deaths, says the Madeira paper should soon be sent, and explains that he is working steadily on his large book without a preliminary essay. He then reports Bosquet’s perfect Chalk Chthamalus drawing, which unsettles his earlier negative geological evidence about Secondary sessile cirripeds.
record_reviews.date_assessment: 10 November 1856; XML bounds 1856-11-10 to 1856-11-10. This boundary record is not period-selection eligible.
record_reviews.attribution_assessment: Darwin-authored outgoing with a distinct opening purpose (answering Lady Lyell via Emma) and a later geological report; Bosquet’s drawing is a reported incoming item, not a preserved letter in this record.
record_reviews.unmatched_reason: No Lyell prompt or Bosquet source text is included; the body supports only Darwin’s report and does not identify a direct incoming endpoint.

evidence.quote: I am writing to you in order to answer Lady Lyells note to Emma
Bosquet of Maestricht sends me a perfect drawing of a perfect Chthamalus

record_reviews.summary: Lyell sends a tabular geological comparison of mammal occurrences, with zeros and counts across Eocene, Chalk, Purbeck, Oolite and Triassic levels. He then says he has casts and drawings of Microlestes from Stuttgart and argues that the absence of angiosperms before Chalk need not predict rarity of warm-blooded quadrupeds. The surviving body is a table-plus-comment sequence ending in an incomplete closing.
record_reviews.date_assessment: 16 January 1857; XML bounds 1857-01-16 to 1857-01-16. This boundary record is not period-selection eligible.
record_reviews.attribution_assessment: Lyell-authored incoming; the numerical table and German “Nochnichtgefundenseyn” are his written material, while casts/drawings are mentioned but no figure node is attached here.
record_reviews.unmatched_reason: Darwin’s question or table request is not preserved; counts and geological argument cannot be assigned to a Darwin reply without that prompt.

evidence.quote: I have casts & beautiful drawings made at my expence when last at Stuttgard
offers no reason to anticipate the rarity of warm blooded quadrupeds

record_reviews.summary: Darwin urges Lyell to influence the Austrian Expedition toward isolated southern islands, dredging in tropical seas, glaciers and erratic boulders, and natural-history collecting. He asks Lyell to recommend his Journal and Volcanic Islands, says little is known of domestic animals in remote countries, and reports a live Helix pomatia surviving seawater baths. The closing adds that he has nothing to suggest Forbes and is pleased by coal-plant and Purbeck fossil news.
record_reviews.date_assessment: 11 February 1857; XML bounds 1857-02-11 to 1857-02-11. This boundary record is not period-selection eligible.
record_reviews.attribution_assessment: Darwin-authored outgoing; expedition plans and reported Lyell news are distinct from completed observations. The Helix experiment is Darwin’s own postscript evidence.
record_reviews.unmatched_reason: No specific Lyell prompt or later reply is preserved; prospective recommendations and a personal experiment do not identify an incoming answer.

evidence.quote: nothing would aid more Natural History, than careful collecting & investigating all the productions of the most insulated islands
I have just had Helix Pomatia quite alive & hearty after 20 days under sea-water

record_reviews.summary: Darwin responds to Lyell’s news of Wollaston’s letter and Madeira paper. He accepts that close faunal similarity is interesting but rejects the claim as proved until insect distribution is understood, while requesting a separate copy of the paper. He then reports ill health and the burden of his species book.
record_reviews.date_assessment: 13 April 1857; XML bounds 1857-04-13 to 1857-04-13. This boundary record is not period-selection eligible.
record_reviews.attribution_assessment: Darwin-authored outgoing; Wollaston’s letter and Lyell’s Madeira paper are reported external sources, not preserved endpoint bodies.
record_reviews.unmatched_reason: Lyell’s preceding letter and Wollaston’s source are not preserved here; the qualified assessment is not enough to reconstruct a direct prompt.

evidence.quote: The news did not require any breaking to me
I am extremely glad to hear that your Madeira paper is making progress

Institutional minutes and reported quotations are preserved with their institutional or third-party voices; they are not silently converted into Darwin letters.
No inline figure nodes were attached to these records; mentions of casts, drawings, plates or specimens remain textual references, not viewed visual evidence.
